newsitem.title: FRANCE: Analysts welcome Worms/Saint Louis merger plan.
newsitem.headline: Analysts welcome Worms/Saint Louis merger plan.

text.p: Analysts on Tuesday welcomed plans by Worms & Cie to merge with Saint-Louis, saying the move will clarify the fate of the paper and sugar group.
They said the transaction would probably lead to asset sales at Saint Louis as financial holding Worms decides on its new development strategy.
Saint Louis, despite its four billion franc war chest of cash, has suffered from a lack of clear strategic goals and several failed expansion attempts, analysts said.
"Saint-Louis was a holding company. It had no strategy. Now there can be some thinking over the future of its main sectors," said Credit Suisse First Boston analyst Anne Alexandre.
She said she was maintaining her 'buy' recommendation on Saint-Louis and on Worms.
"This solution has the merit of ending uncertainties. Now things will happen," another analyst said.
The merger, announced last Friday, will be carried out on the basis of four Worms shares for one Saint-Louis share.
At 1500 GMT Saint Louis was down 0.07 percent at 1,491 francs and Worms was down 1.16 percent at 383.50 francs.
Chairman Daniel Melin, who took the helm of Saint-Louis in May 1995 after then chief Bernard Dumon died in a plane crash, will be replaced by Nicholas Clive Worms, head of Worms & Cie.
Melin tried in vain to convince investors that cash-rich Saint-Louis had a development strategy, analysts said.
But efforts to acquire sugar group Compagnie Francaise de Sucrerie or cocoa processor Cacao Barry failed.
Under Melin the company refocussed on paper and sugar, selling Royal Champignon to Champi Jandou and a remaining stake in prepared-meal unit Panzalim to Danone.

Saint Louis is also trying to be an active player in Spain, acquiring in January a 15 percent stake in Spain's largest sugar company Ebro Agricolas, ahead of the merger of Ebro with the country's second-largest group Azucarera.

Analysts said the merger of Saint Louis and Worms was fuelling new speculation over the fate of the sugar and paper branches but that much hinged on strategic choices made by Worms for its insurance business.
On Monday Worms said it was engaged in a "deep" reflection about the future of its insurance unit Athena.
Since insurer Axa merged last year with rival UAP, signalling a restructuring in the sector, there has been speculation that Worms might sell Athena.
French insurer AGF is often cited as a potential bidder for Athena.
But analysts said Worms may try to strengthen its grip on the insurance business, through the acquisition of a stake in a newly merged AGF-Athena group.
This would force Worms to sell assets to generate the additional cash needed for the transaction.
Some analysts believe that Worms may choose to sell the 40 percent stake Saint Louis has in Arjo Wiggins Appleton, citing the cyclical nature of the paper business.
But others see the Generale Sucriere sugar unit as a natural target for rival sugar group Eridania Beghin-Say.
Prior to the merger Worms controlled 27.8 percent of Saint-Louis and Italy's IFIL SpA, an Agnelli family holding, 26.5 percent. IFIL will have 20 percent of the new company.
